text: A young man joins the campus radicals because that is where the girls are, and for a while the joke is the whole plot. American, 1970, and the film has the strange job of arguing a case it is also standing in the middle of. Stuart Hagmann spends 109 minutes on the mechanism of belief: how someone who arrives with the wrong motive picks up the vocabulary first, then the habits, then something harder to set down. The romance is not a subplot running beside that process but the same process seen from another angle. Whatever the picture makes of the movement it depicts, it is honest about the least flattering fact available, which is that conviction is often contracted socially, from proximity, the way a cold is.

The pool has to be cleaned whether or not there is a war on, and cleaning it is the whole of Adam Ousmane's standing in the world. Then the resort changes hands, the new managers want fewer staff, and the man who takes the job is his son. Mahamat-Saleh Haroun gives this 92 minutes and keeps the Chadian war largely off screen, arriving as demands rather than as fighting: a contribution is expected from every household, and Adam has no money. A French-language production out of Belgium, set at the shallow end of a resort where nothing looks like a country in trouble. The film is exact about what a demotion does to a man of that age. Not poverty. The removal of the one sentence he could say about himself.

Nicholas is a boy who worries about everything, and a week of school skiing gives the worry somewhere to go. Its French title, La Classe de neige, names the institution rather than the story: a trip to the snow, bunk rooms, a coach ride up, other people's children. Claude Miller filmed it in 1998 and files it under mystery, which means he takes the boy's dread at face value instead of treating it as a phase to be outgrown. Ninety-six minutes at child height. The two genres on its card are mystery and drama, and the mystery is lodged inside the child rather than placed in front of him. The unnerving part is not that the visions frighten but that the adults are kind, competent and entirely unequipped, and the ordinary machinery of a supervised holiday keeps running on schedule around a boy it does not reassure.

Crime pictures mostly belong to young men; this one belongs to a gangster old enough that the mistakes have had time to come back. Korea, 2007, 112 minutes, billed as action and comedy as well as crime, and the billing is accurate in an unhappy way, since the comedy lives in the gap between what the man does for money and the domestic life he expects the money to buy. Han Jae-rim is less interested in the trade than in its maintenance: errands, deference to younger bosses, the long accounting of favours owed. It took the Blue Dragon Film Award for Best Film, a fair result for a picture that treats the profession as a job with bad hours. Everything he has done lives in the same house as everything he wanted.

A Korean funeral is a piece of work, and the novelist who comes back to his mother's village finds himself standing in the middle of it for days. He had been writing a fairytale about her dementia, still unpublished when the news arrives, so he mourns a woman he had already begun converting into material. Im Kwon-taek spends 107 minutes on the rites themselves: the arrivals, the drinking, the arguments about precedence, the relatives who use the occasion to reopen older business. Comedy is listed alongside drama and that is not an error. The thing runs for days, and someone has to feed everyone who comes. Grief in a full house is largely logistics, and the village keeps its own accounting, which the son from the city discovers he has forgotten how to read.

The man who comes to take her back does not knock on the door; he takes a job at the kiln and waits. Before that: an old potter saves a young woman's life, she is grateful, she does not love him, and she marries him anyway because she cannot see how to refuse. Korea, 1970, ninety-five minutes, three people and one workplace. The craft is not decoration here. A kiln has to be watched at all hours, and the old man's authority in the film is the authority of someone who knows exactly how long to wait for a thing to finish. The younger man has learned to wait too. It went out as Korea's submission to the Academy Awards, a curious errand for a film this small and this uncomfortable.

The women boarding the liner at Genoa have been promised work abroad, and the man who recruited them is watching from a distance where they cannot see him. German, 1966, eighty-three minutes, and the attention stays with the traffickers rather than the trafficked: Harald, his partner in Berlin, the blackmailer, the competitors who want the route. That choice makes for an uneasy crime picture, since the suspense runs on whether the business survives and the women are its inventory. The port is the last place where the promise still resembles a job. Ernst Hofbauer leaves the machinery fully visible, which is either the film's excuse or its charge. Either way the vocabulary is the point. Recruitment, transport, a partner, competition, a trade described in exactly the terms a legitimate one would use.

Twelfth-century Buddhism in Japan was largely built for men who could afford to leave everything behind. Shingon asked years of demanding practice; Zen offered a blank wall and unceasing sitting; Tendai had metaphysics and systems to study, three long roads laid out for scholars and noblemen with time to spend. Shinran, born in 1173, came to the religion looking for an alternative to the civil wars grinding the country down, and found it arranged for people unlike him. Rentaro Mikuni directs, and takes a hundred and thirty-nine minutes, and the length works as an argument: a film about a path cannot be made in a hurry. The question underneath is social rather than doctrinal, which is who a religion is actually for while the country outside the gate is at war.

Two hours of Indonesia in Ferraniacolor, shot by an Italian crew in 1955 and assembled without a story to carry it. The lost continent of the title is Asia, which fixes the vantage before a frame goes by: a European camera arrives, looks, and calls what it finds lost. A wedding aboard a floating junk, the wheat and rice harvest, sacrifice at the rim of a volcano, a chariot race, dancers in Bali. The list is given rhythm by cutting that behaves as though a plot were running underneath it. Documentary is the only genre named, and it covers a great deal here: travelogue, ethnography, a colour process being shown off at length. Cannes gave it a Special Jury Prize. What lasts is the stock, and the frankness of the arrangement between the filmed and the filming.

A fourth-grader shines shoes after school, keeps his younger brothers calm, and writes the day down in a notebook every night. His father gambles. His mother, unable to bear the man any longer, has gone. What remains is a child running a household on the income of a shoeshine box and recording it, which hands Kim Soo-yong his form: the diary is the boy's ledger and the only place his composure is allowed to slip. Korea, 1965, a hundred and five minutes. The discipline of the film is that it declines to make him pitiable. He has tasks, and he does them, and the brothers must be settled before anything else in the day can start. Whatever weight it asks an audience to carry, it hands over plainly: a boy, a box, an evening, a page.

Yun Sim-deok was famous in Korea in the 1920s for singing, and sixty-odd years later a film gave her a hundred and sixty minutes. The runtime is the first thing worth noticing. Screen biographies of performers usually run to the highlights; this one has room for the intervals between them, the years a summary would drop. Kim Ho-sun made it in 1991, far enough from the period that every room, every coat, every sound of a voice going onto a record had to be rebuilt from evidence rather than recalled. History is the second genre listed, and the film appears to take that as an obligation rather than a setting: the 1920s as a set of conditions a working singer had to live inside, not a wardrobe.

In this village the drowned are said to wait, since a man lost to the sea cannot depart until the sea takes the next one. That is not a metaphor inside the film but a working rule, and a remote stretch of Korea's west coast has to go on living under it. One fisherman drowns and the arithmetic starts. Everybody knows the sum. Chung Jin-woo has ninety-six minutes and a small population, which is enough, because romance is the first genre listed and any attachment between two people here has the village's accounting running underneath it. The grip of the premise is that nobody needs to enforce the belief. It is simply what is known, the way weather is known, and it works through people who would each say they meant no harm.

A country declared its independence and kept it for three days, which is either a footnote or a film. Shin Sang-ok chose the film and gave it a hundred and thirty-two minutes, most of them necessarily spent before the three days begin, on the argument itself: men who wanted Korea to stay with China against men who had been reading westward and looking to Japan. Kim Okgyun is the reformer who talks a king into it. The difficulty of the material is that it holds no innocent faction, and the conservative who carries word to China is not, in the terms of the period, betraying anything. Each side believes it is the one saving the country. The last years of the Yi dynasty are a large subject, and this takes the narrowest window available onto them.
